content: The datasets mentioned can be utilized as inputs for mathematical models, which allow for the estimation of infection rates and the burden of chronic infections. Several countries have successfully implemented these analytical methods. Cascade data can be estimated from existing treatment cohorts, as most patients are treated at tertiary centers where comprehensive historical data is available. Hospital data from tertiary gastroenterology centers can be used to evaluate the proportion of diagnosed individuals receiving treatment and to assess treatment outcomes, including viral suppression, cure rates, hepatitis-related complications (such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cirrhosis), and mortality rates. Reporting of chronic hepatitis B and C cases in healthcare facilities can also help estimate the number of cases identified and managed within healthcare services. This information is critical for assessing care or cure cascades and for generating assumptions relevant to specific settings, which can then be applied in modeling estimates of disease burden. However, it is important to note that modeling based on healthcare facility data may not provide a robust method for estimating disease burden, as many individuals with chronic hepatitis infections do not seek medical care. Additionally, repeated visits to healthcare facilities may result in duplicate reporting, which must be addressed through deduplication processes. Countries should regularly consolidate, deduplicate, and update these datasets. Core indicators of the diagnosis and treatment cascade can be estimated more efficiently using aggregated data reported from all healthcare facilities involved in hepatitis treatment, including tertiary and teaching hospitals in both public and private sectors. Aggregated data management is less labor-intensive and is particularly suitable for programs in the early stages of scaling up. Drug manufacturer consumption data can also serve as a major source for estimating treatment numbers in a country. This data can be triangulated with logistics management information systems and manufacturer consumption data (including private sector data). While these datasets may not align perfectly, they can provide insights into levels, trends, and geographic variations. Hepatitis data from the above steps can be used by countries for planning, reporting, and management purposes. Gaps in data can be addressed through modeling, and investment cases can be developed as needed. Countries with limited data may rely on mathematical models to complement empirical data for estimating the prevalence, incidence, and mortality of viral hepatitis. However, these models have limitations and may lack accuracy. Modeling should always be used to extend data rather than as a standalone activity. Similarly, data sources often require triangulation and extrapolation to be useful for estimation, such as when a prevalence survey is outdated or needs to be age-standardized to the total population. Information on antiviral agents and their consumption can complement this data and enable adjustments for private clinic data. Countries should also plan to address data gaps and weaknesses while strengthening data systems for the future. Hepatitis programs can leverage existing case surveillance systems to monitor the care cascade, from individual patient monitoring at the facility level to aggregate reporting at the central level. Databases of individuals with chronic infections can provide longitudinal data based on individual records. Individual patient records are essential tools in patient care, supporting longitudinal monitoring and improving the quality and continuity of care by ensuring that multiple aspects of healthcare are visible to providers over time. This includes related infections, treatment gaps, or other aspects requiring follow-up. Similarly, tracking prevention services (such as pre-exposure prophylaxis or harm-reduction services) at the individual level benefits from the ability to observe individual-level data. However, data entry and management of databases containing individual patient records are resource-intensive. Countries need to enhance the analysis of outcomes to improve the estimation of the burden of hepatitis B and C and to assess hepatitis-related complications. This can be implemented in selected sentinel tertiary reference centers, particularly in countries where treatment and care for viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma are provided in specialized centers (such as oncology clinics, hepatology or gastroenterology centers, and tertiary hospitals). This analysis involves determining the prevalence of hepatitis B and C among cases of decompensated cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. By using case report forms, treatment centers can extract data on hepatitis B or C diagnoses, as well as diagnoses with cirrhosis (including decompensated cirrhosis, if possible) and hepatocellular carcinoma. Extracted data can also include demographic characteristics such as age and sex, HDV coinfection status, and other potential risk factors for liver disease, including alcohol consumption and metabolic syndromes (such as diabetes and dyslipidemia). Multiplying the estimated number of deaths from decompensated cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver failure by the fractions of sequelae attributable to hepatitis B and C can provide an estimate of the disease burden. Countries should use all available data to scale up viral hepatitis prevention and treatment services. This includes leveraging HBV/HCV burden and cascade data, which are available for most countries. Strengthening the analysis of outcomes through cancer registries, death registries, and sentinel sites for mortality attributable to HBV and HCV is essential. Integrating hepatitis diagnosis and treatment data into health management information systems or district health information systems for routine use, where relevant and with interoperability, is also critical.
